how.d: Short, plain-English explanations — no grammar walls, no jargon without a translation.
Each phrase speaks in a native Tamil voice. Slow it to 0.2× and repeat until it sticks.
Every topic ends in practice: quiz yourself, then review the words until they stay.

hfaqs.a: No. Start with spoken Tamil in Roman letters, and let the script come second. Learners who speak first stay motivated far longer than learners who drill letters for a month before saying a word.
hfaqs.q: Must I learn the Tamil script before speaking?

hfaqs.a: வணக்கம் for respect, ஆம் and இல்லை, நன்றி, தயவுசெய்து, சரி, and நான் — I. With those seven you can open any interaction in Tamil Nadu politely while your vocabulary grows underneath.
hfaqs.q: Which words should I learn in week one?

hfaqs.a: The Dravidian sounds new to most ears — ழ் (zh), the rolled ர, the three n's and l's. Ten minutes of daily listening retunes your ears within weeks; the pronunciation page walks you through each one.
hfaqs.q: What is the hardest part of Tamil?

topics.desc: வணக்கம் opens every door in Tamil Nadu — plus mornings, welcomes and warm goodbyes. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Yes, and nobody will mind — வணக்கம் with folded hands is understood and loved everywhere Tamil is spoken. With close friends a smile and நலமா? (nalamaa — are you well?) feels warmer.
faqs.q: Can I just say vanakkam everywhere?

faqs.a: வணக்கம் with folded hands and a small nod, and நீங்கள் (neenga — formal you) until invited closer. Add அண்ணா (annaa) or அக்கா (akkaa) for someone slightly older — it warms everything instantly.
faqs.q: How do I greet an elder respectfully?

faqs.a: பிறகு பார்க்கலாம் (piragu paarkkalaam — we'll meet again later) is the warm standard. சென்று வாருங்கள் (sendru vaarungal — go and come back) is the classic elder's farewell — receive it with a smile and a nod.
faqs.q: How do Tamils say goodbye?

topics.note: A note on நலமா vs சௌக்கியமா. நலமா? (nalamaa) is the everyday are you well? — warm, quick, everywhere. சௌக்கியமா? (saukkiyamaa) is its formal elder cousin, heard at weddings and festivals. Start with நலமா; graduate to சௌக்கியமா when aunties adopt you.
paras: வணக்கம் (vanakkam) is the one greeting that never fails. Folded hands, a small nod, and it works with strangers, elders, shopkeepers and officials — exactly the people a learner meets first. Say it clearly, hold the folded hands half a second, and Tamil Nadu opens to you.

Mornings get their own greeting: காலை வணக்கம் (kaalai vanakkam — good morning), heard in offices, schools and tea stalls until about eleven. Evenings soften to மாலை வணக்கம் (maalai vanakkam). Time-stamped greetings signal that you live in the language, not just visit it.

Welcomes are grand in Tamil culture: வாருங்கள் (vaarungal — please come/welcome) opens homes, shops and hearts. Guests are greeted standing, often with water or coffee before a single question. Return the warmth — வந்துவிட்டேன், நன்றி (I've come, thank you) — and you are family within minutes.

Goodbyes promise return, never end: பிறகு பார்க்கலாம் (we'll meet again later) is the everyday farewell; பார்த்துக்கொள்ளுங்கள் (take care) adds affection. Leave every conversation with a வணக்கம் and a smile — in Tamil Nadu, how you leave is remembered longer than how you came.
topics.title: Saying hello the Tamil way

topics.desc: 12 vowels, 18 consonants and the famous ழ் — the Tamil alphabet without tears. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Twelve vowels (உயிர்), eighteen consonants (மெய்), one aytham (ஃ) — 31 letters that combine into 247 total shapes. Sounds huge, behaves simply: learn the 12 + 18 and the combinations assemble themselves.
faqs.q: How many letters does Tamil have?

faqs.a: ழ் (zh) — a sound between r, l and d made with the tongue curled back. தமிழ் itself contains it, so every Tamil learner must conquer it. Listen, curl, practise: it arrives within weeks.
faqs.q: What is the hardest Tamil letter?

faqs.a: No — Tamil has no aspirated consonants (no kh, gh, th, bh). One க covers ka, kha, ga and gha by position. Fewer letters to learn, smarter rules to love.
faqs.q: Does Tamil have kh, gh, bh sounds?

topics.note: A note on the pulli (்). The tiny dot above a consonant kills its hidden vowel: க is ka, க் is just k. Tamil writes pure consonants with the pulli and syllables without — க் + அ = க. One dot, and the whole reading system clicks.
paras: Tamil vowels (உயிர் எழுத்து — life letters) come in twelve: அ ஆ இ ஈ உ ஊ எ ஏ ஐ ஒ ஓ ஔ, plus the special ஃ (aytham). Short and long pairs — அ/ஆ, இ/ஈ, உ/ஊ — change meaning completely: கல் (kal — stone) versus கால் (kaal — leg). Length is meaning in Tamil; stretch with care.

Consonants (மெய் எழுத்து — body letters) number eighteen: க் ங் ச் ஞ் ட் ண் த் ந் ப் ம் ய் ர் ல் வ் ழ் ள் ற் ன். Notice what's missing: no aspirates, no separate voiced letters. One letter per mouth position, pronounced soft or hard by rule — Tamil spelling is famously faithful to speech.

Vowels and consonants marry into உயிர்மெய் (uyirmei) combinations: க் + அ = க (ka), க் + ஆ = கா (kaa). Twelve vowels times eighteen consonants gives 216 combos plus the 31 originals — 247 shapes from simple, predictable joins. Learn the joins, not the list.

Then the crown jewel: ழ் (zh), the retroflex approximant Tamil is famous for — தமிழ், வாழ்க்கை, பழம். Curl the tongue back without touching the roof, voice it, and feel the most Tamil sound in existence. Natives will grin when you land it; the grin is worth weeks of practice.
topics.title: Tamil alphabet

topics.desc: ஒன்று இரண்டு மூன்று to நூறு — plus clock time and the ancient Tamil digits. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Both, mixed freely — but learn international digits for daily life (prices, phones, buses all use them) and recognise Tamil digits (௦௧௨௩...) for temples, invitations and proverbs. The ancient digits survive in ceremony, not commerce.
faqs.q: Tamil digits or international digits?

faqs.a: Take the number, add மணி (mani — bell/hour): மூன்று மணி (three o'clock). Half past adds அரை (arai) — மூன்றரை மணி is half past three. One rule, every clock in Tamil Nadu.
faqs.q: How do I say the time in Tamil?

faqs.a: எவ்வளவு? (evvalavu — how much?). Then listen for the number plus ரூபாய் (roobaai — rupees). Market Tamil is the fastest teacher there is.
faqs.q: How do I ask the price?

topics.note: A note on ௦௧௨௩௪௫௬௭௮௯. Tamil has its own ancient digits — ௧ ௨ ௩ ௪ ௫ ௬ ௭ ௮ ௯ ௰ ௱ ௲ — beautiful and nearly retired. You'll meet them on temple walls and wedding invitations. Learn to recognise them for joy; use international digits for life.
paras: One to ten: ஒன்று (ondru), இரண்டு (irandu), மூன்று (moondru), நான்கு (naangu), ஐந்து (aindu), ஆறு (aaru), ஏழு (eezhu), எட்டு (ettu), ஒன்பது (onbadu), பத்து (patthu). Chant them in rhythm — Tamil numbers love rhythm — and they stick in days, not weeks.

Eleven to nineteen build on பத்து: பதினொன்று (11), பன்னிரண்டு (12), பதிமூன்று (13)... then the tens march: இருபது (20), முப்பது (30), நாற்பது (40), ஐம்பது (50), அறுபது (60), எழுபது (70), எண்பது (80), தொண்ணூறு (90), நூறு (100). Past twenty, glue tens to units — இருபத்து ஒன்று (21) — and count to a thousand (ஆயிரம்) without fear.

Money runs on numbers: the currency is the ரூபாய் (roobaai — rupee), and எவ்வளவு? (evvalavu — how much?) is the most useful sentence in Tamil Nadu. Listen for the number, repeat it back — ஐம்பது? (fifty?) — and your first Tamil transaction completes itself.

Time reuses numbers with மணி (mani — hour): இரண்டு மணி (two o'clock), ஐந்து மணி (five o'clock). இப்போது மணி என்ன? (ippodu mani enna — what time is it now?) is the question; half hours add அரை (arai — half). Numbers, money, clocks: one skill, three daily victories.
topics.title: Counting in Tamil

topics.desc: Names, homes and small talk — your first real Tamil conversations, line by line. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: உங்கள் பெயர் என்ன? (ungal peyar enna — what is your name?) for respect; உன் பெயர் என்ன? (un peyar enna) for friends and children. Answer with என் பெயர்... (en peyar — my name is...). Names first, always.
faqs.q: How do I ask someone's name?

faqs.a: நீங்கள் எங்கிருந்து வருகிறீர்கள்? (where are you from?) — then answer for yourself: நான் ... இருந்து வருகிறேன். Origin questions are the universal second question; prepare your answer before you need it.
faqs.q: How do I say where I'm from?

faqs.a: மெதுவாகப் பேசுங்கள் (please speak slowly) and மீண்டும் சொல்லுங்கள் (please say it again). Said with a smile, these two sentences make every Tamil speaker slow down and help.
faqs.q: What do I say when people speak too fast?

topics.note: A note on நீங்கள், நீ and the missing middle. Tamil has two yous where English has one: நீங்கள் (neenga — formal/plural) and நீ (nee — familiar). No three-level ladder like Bengali — just respect versus closeness. Start with நீங்கள் for every adult; let friendship invite you to நீ.
paras: Every first conversation follows the same dance: வணக்கம், உங்கள் பெயர் என்ன? (what is your name?), என் பெயர்... (my name is...), நீங்கள் எங்கிருந்து வருகிறீர்கள்? (where are you from?). Four lines, and you have had a real conversation. Practise them in order until they flow without thinking.

Small talk runs on three questions: நீங்கள் என்ன செய்கிறீர்கள்? (what do you do?), தமிழ் பேசுவீர்களா? (do you speak Tamil?), சாப்பிட்டீர்களா? (have you eaten? — asked with genuine care). Answer briefly, ask back immediately — உங்களுக்கு? நீங்கள்? — because conversations are volleys, not speeches.

When the torrent comes — and Tamil hospitality pours words — deploy the brakes: மெதுவாகப் பேசுங்கள் (please speak slowly), எனக்குப் புரியவில்லை (I don't understand), மீண்டும் சொல்லுங்கள் (please say it again). Every Tamil speaker honours these instantly; they are the learner's seatbelt.

Close warmly and promise return: உங்களைச் சந்தித்ததில் மகிழ்ச்சி (pleased to meet you), மீண்டும் சந்திப்போம் (we'll meet again), பிறகு பார்க்கலாம் (see you later). Leave with a வணக்கம் and the door stays open — Tamil conversations end the way they begin: with folded hands.
topics.title: Real Tamil conversation

topics.desc: போ, வா, சாப்பிடு — the twelve verbs that run daily life, plus how they bend. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Stems are orders to friends — போ! (go!), வா! (come!), சாப்பிடு! (eat!). Polite speech adds endings: போங்கள் (please go), வாருங்கள் (please come). Learn stems first, politeness second, and never order a stranger.
faqs.q: Are verb stems commands?

faqs.a: நான் போகிறேன் (I go), நீ போகிறாய் (you go), அவர் போகிறார் (he/she formal goes). Person-markers on every verb — நான்/நீ/அவர் each pull their own ending. Drill one verb through all persons and the pattern owns you.
faqs.q: How do Tamil verbs change?

faqs.a: இல்லை (illai — no/not) negates nouns and adjectives — எனக்குத் தெரியாது uses -ஆது for verbs (I don't know). Tamil negation splits by word type; learn இல்லை for things, வேண்டாம் (vendaam — don't want) for refusals.
faqs.q: How do I say no to a verb?

topics.note: A note on வாருங்கள் vs வா. வா (vaa) orders a friend to come; வாருங்கள் (vaarungal) welcomes a guest like royalty. Same verb, different universe — the -ங்கள் ending is pure respect. When in doubt, add the respect: Tamils forgive stiff politeness instantly and casual rudeness never.
paras: Twelve verbs carry daily life: போ (go), வா (come), சாப்பிடு (eat), குடி (drink), படி (read/study), எழுது (write), செய் (do), பேசு (speak), கொடு (give), எடு (take), இரு (be/stay), பார் (see). Memorise these stems and you can order food, find toilets, make friends and survive beautifully.

Stems bend by person in the present: நான் போகிறேன் (I go), நீ போகிறாய் (you familiar go), நீங்கள் போகிறீர்கள் (you formal go), அவர் போகிறார் (he/she formal goes). The -கிற- (kira) infix marks present tense across nearly every verb — one infix, hundreds of verbs, instant sentences.

Polite commands add -ங்கள்: போங்கள் (please go), வாருங்கள் (please come), சாப்பிடுங்கள் (please eat), சொல்லுங்கள் (please say). This one ending turns every order into an invitation — it is the most useful suffix in Tamil, worth more than a hundred nouns.

Negation and existence close the kit: இருக்கிறது (irukkiradhu — it is / there is) anchors locations — புத்தகம் மேசையில் இருக்கிறது (the book is on the table). இல்லை (illai — there isn't) removes — பணம் இல்லை (no money). Twelve verbs plus இருக்கிறது/இல்லை: the engine room of Tamil.

topics.desc: Water, money, time, today — the everyday Tamil words that unlock daily life. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Time words first: இன்று (today), நாளை (tomorrow), நேற்று (yesterday), இப்போது (now). You will use them ten times a day — shopping, planning, chatting — while rare nouns gather dust.
faqs.q: Which words pay off fastest?

faqs.a: Tamil happily absorbs English — பஸ் (bus), டிக்கெட் (ticket), ஆபீஸ் (office). Use the pure Tamil word when you know it (பேருந்து, நுழைவுச்சீட்டு), the loanword when you don't. Fluency first, purity later.
faqs.q: Is mixing English okay?

faqs.a: Nouns first, verbs second, adjectives third. With fifty nouns and the twelve verbs from the verbs page, you can point, ask and survive — grammar glues them later.
faqs.q: Nouns or verbs first?

topics.note: A note on இன்று, நாளை, நேற்று. Tamil time words pivot around today: இன்று (indru — today), நாளை (naalai — tomorrow), நேற்று (nettru — yesterday). Master this trio and half your daily sentences assemble themselves — நாளை பார்க்கலாம் (see you tomorrow) alone is worth the lesson.
paras: Survival runs on nouns: தண்ணீர் (thanneer — water), உணவு (unavu — food), வீடு (veedu — home), பணம் (panam — money), நேரம் (neram — time). Five words, and you can ask for water, find home, handle money and ask the time — the entire first day in a new city.

Movement words come next: சாலை (saalai — road), பேருந்து (perundu — bus), கடை (kadai — shop), பள்ளி (palli — school). Tamil cities move by bus and foot; knowing பேருந்து நிலையம் எங்கே? (where is the bus stand?) saves more time than any app.

Opinions need adjectives: நல்ல (nalla — good), பெரிய (periya — big), சிறிய (siriya — small), புதிய (pudiya — new), பழைய (pazhaya — old). நல்லது (nalladhu — that's good) approves everything from food to plans — the most useful single opinion in Tamil.

Weather and mood close the kit: மழை (mazhai — rain) matters half the year, வெயில் (veyil — sun/heat) the other half. மழை வருகிறது (rain is coming) starts conversations with strangers; in Tamil Nadu, weather talk is friendship's front door.

topics.desc: Idli, dosai, filter kaapi — order like a local, from breakfast to bill. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Point and say இது ஒன்று (idhu ondru — one of these) — it works in every mess, canteen and bakery in Tamil Nadu. Add தயவுசெய்து (please) and a smile; grammar can wait until dessert.
faqs.q: How do I order with almost no Tamil?

faqs.a: காரம் குறைவாக (kaaram kuraivaaga — less spicy, please). Tamil food honours chilli deeply; this one sentence saves sensitive stomachs while keeping every flavour.
faqs.q: How do I ask for less spicy food?

faqs.a: ருசியாக இருக்கிறது (rusiyaaga irukkiradhu — it's delicious). Say it to the cook, the server, the auntie who packed your lunch — it is the highest compliment in Tamil food culture.
faqs.q: How do I praise the food?

topics.note: A note on காபி. Filter kaapi — strong decoction, frothed milk, drunk from the dabara-tumbler — is not coffee, it is a morning ritual. Order ஒரு காபி (oru kaapi — one coffee) at any stall, watch it cool mid-air between vessels, and understand Tamil Nadu in one sip.
paras: Breakfast is the glory: இட்லி (idli — steamed rice cakes), தோசை (dosai — crisp crepe), பொங்கல் (pongal — rice-lentil comfort), வடை (vadai — savoury doughnut), all served with சாம்பார் (saambaar) and சட்னி (chutney). டிபன் சாப்பிட்டீர்களா? (have you had tiffin?) is asked with love — answer honestly, then accept seconds.

Meals centre on சாப்பாடு (saappaadu — the rice meal): rice, சாம்பார், ரசம் (rasam — pepper-tamarind soup), கூட்டு (koottu — lentil-vegetable), தயிர் (tayir — curd), அப்பளம் (appalam — crisp papad). Served on banana leaves at weddings, eaten with the right hand — சாப்பாடு ரெடியா? (is the meal ready?) is the happiest question.

Taste words steer every order: காரம் (kaaram — spicy), இனிப்பு (inippu — sweet), புளிப்பு (pulippu — sour), உப்பு (uppu — salt). கொஞ்சம் உப்பு (a little salt), சர்க்கரை வேண்டாம் (no sugar) — with taste words, your plate obeys you.

Drinks and bills close the meal: காபி (filter coffee), தேநீர் (theneer — tea), மோர் (moor — buttermilk), பழச்சாறு (pazhachcharu — juice). கணக்கு கொடுங்கள் (kanakku kodungal — please give the bill) ends it; ருசியாக இருந்தது (it was delicious) guarantees a smile on your way out.

topics.desc: ழ், three n's, two r's — every tricky Tamil sound, one by one, with examples. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Yes — ந் (alveolar, like English n), ன் (dental, tongue on teeth), ண் (retroflex, tongue curled back). மன் (man — mind/mud) versus மண் (mann — soil) is a real minimal pair; natives hear the difference instantly.
faqs.q: Does Tamil really have three n sounds?

faqs.a: ர is a light flap (like the dd in American cuter); ற is a hard trill (rolled r). மரம் (maram — tree) versus மறம்? — flap soft, trill strong. Practise மரம் daily; the flap arrives first.
faqs.q: What is the difference between ர and ற?

faqs.a: Dental consonants touch the teeth (த், ந்), retroflexes curl the tongue back (ட், ண்). தரம் (tharam — quality) versus டமாரம்? — teeth versus roof. Exaggerate at first; subtlety follows.
faqs.q: Dental versus retroflex — help?

topics.note: A note on ழ் (zh). Tamil's signature sound: curl the tongue back toward the roof WITHOUT touching, and voice it — between r, l and a French j. தமிழ், பழம், வாழ்க்கை. Children take years to perfect it, so forgive yourself months — then enjoy the applause.
paras: The three n's sort by tongue position: ந் (alveolar — English-like n, as in நல்ல), ன் (dental — tongue on teeth, as in மீன்), ண் (retroflex — curled back, as in கண்). Say na-na-na sliding the tongue from ridge to teeth to roof — three letters, one glide.

The two r's split soft and hard: ர் is a single flap — மரம் (maram — tree), பெரிய (periya — big) — while ற் trills hard — பறவை (paravai — bird), வெற்றி (verri — victory). English ears merge them; Tamil meaning doesn't. Practise pairs daily until your tongue files them separately.

Dental versus retroflex stops: த் (teeth — தமிழ், தண்ணீர்) against ட் (roof — படம், வீடு). Hold a finger to your lips: dentals puff forward, retroflexes pop upward. Ten minutes of த-ட alternation retunes the mouth within a week.

The rest behave kindly: ச is cha at word start (சாப்பாடு) softening to sa inside words (பேசு), க hardens and softens by position (கடை, மகன்), and long vowels simply hold double — ஆ, ஈ, ஊ. Tamil spelling mirrors speech faithfully: pronounce what you see, and you are right nine times in ten.

topics.desc: Verb last, respect built in — Tamil grammar in plain English, no jargon walls. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Put the verb last: நான் புத்தகம் படிக்கிறேன் (I book read). Subject-Object-Verb, always. English instincts will fight you for a week; then SOV feels like home.
faqs.q: Where does the verb go?

faqs.a: எனக்கு (enakku — to me), உனக்கு (unakku — to you familiar), உங்களுக்கு (ungalukku — to you formal). எனக்கு தண்ணீர் வேண்டும் (I want water) is literally to-me water is-wanted — Tamil wants flow toward people.
faqs.q: How do I say I want something?

faqs.a: இது (idhu — this, near me), அது (adhu — that, far). இது என்ன? (what is this?) points at anything within reach; mastery takes one shopping trip.
faqs.q: How do this and that work?

topics.note: A note on -க்கு (kku). Tamil's dative ending aims verbs at people and places: எனக்கு (to me), பள்ளிக்கு (to school), வீட்டுக்கு (homeward). Sentences like எனக்குப் புரிகிறது (to-me it-is-understood = I understand) reveal Tamil's worldview: experiences come TO you.
paras: Tamil sentences end with the verb: நான் புத்தகம் படிக்கிறேன் (I — book — read). Subject first, object middle, verb last — SOV, the order of half the world's languages. Rearrange your English instincts once, and every Tamil sentence parses cleanly.

Small endings do heavy work: -இல் (il — in/on) places things — வீட்டில் (at home), மேசையில் (on the table); -உடன் (udan — with) joins company — நண்பருடன் (with a friend); -க்கு (kku) aims motion and wanting — பள்ளிக்கு (to school), எனக்கு வேண்டும் (I want). Endings, not word order, carry Tamil meaning.

Questions rise at the end: நீங்கள் எங்கே போகிறீர்கள்? (where are you going?) — எங்கே (where), என்ன (what), யார் (who), ஏன் (why), எப்படி (how), எப்போது (when). Yes-no questions add -ஆ (-aa): சாப்பிட்டீர்களா? (have you eaten?). Question words plus rising tone — asking is easy.

Negation splits three ways: இல்லை (illai) denies existence — பணம் இல்லை (no money); verb endings deny actions — எனக்குத் தெரியாது (I don't know); வேண்டாம் (vendaam) refuses — சர்க்கரை வேண்டாம் (no sugar, thanks). Three no's for three jobs — Tamil refuses precisely.
